claims.text: The baseline material is a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The as-processed baseline has a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state.
The proposed intervention is high-temperature annealing in an inert atmosphere.
The intervention should be conducted at 400–600 °C for 1–5 hours in argon or nitrogen.
Annealing in an inert atmosphere introduces a controlled amount of oxygen into the alloy system.
The intervention forms a stable, protective oxide layer on the alloy surface.
The annealing treatment may refine the alloy's grain structure.
The protective oxide layer improves corrosion resistance.
The protective oxide layer improves resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
Annealing-induced grain refinement can improve the alloy's mechanical properties.
The treatment improves room-temperature compressive behavior relative to the as-processed baseline.
The treatment enhances corrosion resistance relative to the as-processed baseline.
The treatment increases high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-processed baseline.
The optimal annealing temperature, duration, and atmosphere for the specific alloy are unknown.
The hypothesis can be tested by varying annealing temperature and time and comparing microstructure, compression behavior, and corrosion performance with the as-processed baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires controlled oxygen introduction and oxide formation, but the stated intervention and boundaries specify only annealing in an inert atmosphere and provide no oxygen source, oxygen partial pressure, or dosing method.
